About

I’m a Master of Computer Science student at Johns Hopkins University, interested in AI agents, AI infrastructure, and LLM inference.

I’m interested in AI engineering that makes everyday work easier. My experience spans DynaFace, a SwiftUI app for facial palsy assessment; training a 64M-parameter language model from scratch; and building a multi-step AI agent with Spring AI.

    Experience

    DynaFace Mobile

    2026.03 – 2026.07

    Graduate Software Engineer · Johns Hopkins University Medicine

    Built the iOS app in SwiftUI for an AI tool that scores facial palsy from a patient’s video, used by patients and clinicians at Johns Hopkins University Medicine.

    Illustrative use case

    An at-home recording, ready for the follow-up visit

    A patient records a 12-second smile clip. The app turns the upload into an annotated video and a five-area report for the clinician to review.

    Implementation details

    • Owned the full capture-to-result flow: guided video recording, upload, cloud inference, annotated video, and a five-area facial function scorecard.
    • Built email verification, password reset, account deletion, and patient controls to hide their data from selected clinicians.
    • Designed a serverless Firebase and Google Cloud backend with asynchronous video jobs, targeting capacity for 1,000–2,000 patients.

    Projects

    MiniMind

    2026.03 – 2026.06

    Trained a 64M-parameter language model from scratch through pre-training, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), LoRA, DPO, and GRPO.

    Python · PyTorch · LoRA · DPO · GRPO

    Implementation details

    • Implemented and analyzed core Transformer components including RMSNorm, RoPE, and Grouped Query Attention (GQA).
    • Fine-tuned for multi-turn conversation and evaluated differences across pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and preference alignment.
    • Explored inference optimizations including KV caching and attention memory efficiency.

    Training process

    Dinner planning, from data to deployment.

    Scroll sideways to follow the full training map.

    01
    Data
    1 / 8
    PrepareChoose useful conversations

    Collect everyday requests and helpful replies. Keep test conversations separate.

    “I have rice, chickpeas, tomatoes and spinach. Plan a dairy-free dinner for two in 20 minutes, using one pan, with leftovers for tomorrow.”
    02
    Pretrain
    2 / 8
    Learn languageLearn language first

    Read broad text and learn how words fit together.

    Recipes, conversations and general writing teach language; this one dinner request is only an illustration.
    03
    SFT
    3 / 8
    Learn from examplesLearn to ask and answer

    Practice helpful conversations, including questions that resolve missing information.

    Assistant: “Is the rice cooked?” User: “Yes.” Assistant: “Make a tomato-chickpea rice skillet; add spinach last.”
    04
    LoRA
    4 / 8
    Optional branchPractice a specialty

    Optionally tune small adapters for a narrower task.

    Practice cooking requests with ingredient, time and dietary constraints.
    05
    DPO
    5 / 8
    Alignment option APrefer the better reply

    Learn from chosen and rejected responses.

    Prefer a dairy-free, one-pan plan over a reply that adds cheese or needs an oven.
    06
    GRPO
    6 / 8
    Alignment option BCompare several attempts

    Score candidate plans with a task rubric and review their usefulness.

    Check ingredients, dairy avoidance, timing and equipment. These checks need more judgment than an exact math answer.
    07
    Evaluate
    7 / 8
    Check and improveTry unfamiliar requests

    Evaluate new conversations and use mistakes to guide another training pass.

    Change the ingredients or equipment. Does the model adapt its plan and ask when something is unclear?
    08
    Export
    8 / 8
    Ready for inferenceSave and use

    Save the model and tokenizer, then try a fresh conversation.

    Follow-up: “I have no spinach.” A useful reply adapts the dish instead of repeating the original plan.

    Agent workflow

    “Can I book Cedar for 90 minutes?”

    Scroll sideways to follow the loop.

    01
    Understand
    1 / 6
    Round 1Choose evidence

    Look up the room’s booking rules.

    Needed: the maximum booking duration.
    02
    Retrieve
    2 / 6
    Round 1Search documents

    The first result describes equipment, but gives no time limit.

    “Cedar has a display and whiteboard.”
    03
    Check
    3 / 6
    Round 1Spot gaps

    Return the result to the model and keep track of what is missing.

    Missing: how long a booking can last.
    04
    Refine
    4 / 6
    Round 2Search again

    Use that feedback to make the next search more specific.

    Cedar booking duration → “Maximum: 60 minutes.”
    05
    Answer
    5 / 6
    Round 2Cite policy

    Answer using the retrieved rule.

    “No. Cedar allows up to 60 minutes per booking.”
    06
    Improve
    6 / 6
    Proposed · EvaluationTest changes

    Save failed cases, adjust retrieval instructions, and rerun the checks.

    Regression check: a 90-minute request must mention the 60-minute limit.
